clue.text: Sticks foot in new Nikes

indicators.note: new tells us the trainer brand's letters are made anew in a different order

parts.note: taken as written, the fodder to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone shoves a foot into a fresh pair of Nike trainers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'in' does double duty in the surface but here simply sits between the foot and the shoes: F goes inside the rearranged brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: To knife someone is to stab them, and sticks is a verb for stabbing with a blade.

clue.text: A lack of wordplay raised obstacle; one in 9?

parts.note: no, as in no money, means a lack

indicators.note: in a down answer raising a word turns it upside down, reading it bottom to top

parts.note: a pun is a play on words
a let is a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance'

explanation.surface: A grumble that a puzzle lacks wordplay, posed as a riddle about nine.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonuplet is one of nine children born at a single birth, like a twin or triplet.

clue.text: Fine steak one dressed badly

parts.note: rump is a cut of steak

explanation.surface: A good steak served by someone shabbily dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: A frump is a dowdy person who wears unfashionable, unattractive clothing.

clue.text: Chips aren't digested without a ___

indicators.note: digested food is broken down, so these letters are broken up and reassembled
without means the letter a is left out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe ignored
the clue's own a is the single letter the shuffled fodder must lose

explanation.surface: A cheeky fill-in-the-blank about where chips end up after digestion.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is the definition, and the whole clue is the wordplay; the anagram fodder holds one more letter than the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The anal sphincter is the ring of muscle that controls what leaves the digestive tract.

clue.text: Flee horror film after a word to the cameraman

indicators.note: after puts the film's title behind the photographer's word in the answer

parts.note: people posing for a photo are told to say 'cheese' to make them smile
It is the Stephen King horror film about a clown

explanation.surface: An actor runs from the set of a horror film after a word with the camera operator.
explanation.walkthrough: CHEESE IT is old slang shouted to mean 'run for it!', so the definition is an imperative.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang exclamation urges escape, equivalent to telling someone to run away or scram.

clue.text: Tea not quite hot in French cups — it's a wine place

indicators.note: cups means holds, as hands cup something, so the French word goes around
not quite means the French word loses its final letter

parts.note: chaud is the French for hot
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lukewarm tea served in French cups at a vineyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bordeaux château is a wine-producing estate, its name often on the label.

clue.text: Duck on rolls to follow feast

indicators.note: to follow places the reversed word after the feast

parts.note: Eid is a Muslim festival or feast

indicators.note: rolls turns the short word over so it reads backwards

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: Duck, with bread rolls, to finish a feast.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a large sea duck prized for its soft down.

clue.text: 5A confused greedy head of Benenden

parts.note: 5A's answer splits as CHEESE IT; the cheese is the definition, and IT means sex appeal, SA

indicators.note: confused mixes up the letters of greedy

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written; Benenden is an English girls' boarding school

explanation.surface: A cross-reference grumble about a greedy headmistress of Benenden, a private girls' school in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: 5A is used twice: its first word, CHEESE, is the definition, and its second, IT, stands for sex appeal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage Derby is an English cheese marbled green with sage.

clue.text: Popular delicacy not eaten up at all

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
tact is delicacy in dealing with people

explanation.surface: A popular delicacy left completely untouched on the plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' suggests a fancy food; here it is the sensitivity sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Something intact is whole and undamaged, with no part consumed or removed.

clue.text: "When"?

definitions.meaning: what a guest says when the host is pouring a drink, to say stop
flags that the single word stands for a whole phrase it means

explanation.walkthrough: When someone pours you a drink you say 'when' to mean you have had plenty; the answer is a stock phrase with the same force.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the toast-time 'when' and the stock phrase signal that no more is needed or wanted.

clue.text: Dress returned by husband — he prefers to wear black

indicators.note: by means next to, so the husband's letter sits alongside the reversed clothing word
returned sends the dressing word back the other way

parts.note: to tog up is to dress, as in togs for clothes

explanation.surface: A husband hands back a dress because he would rather wear black himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A goth belongs to a subculture known for dark clothing and black makeup.

clue.text: Drug supplier putting something to smoke in Englishman's case

indicators.note: in puts the smoking item inside the case

parts.note: the outside letters of the word Englishman, its first and last, form a case
a pipe is smoked with tobacco

explanation.surface: Someone tucks a pipe into an Englishman's carry case, as if supplying contraband.
explanation.definitionFit: An EpiPen is an auto-injector that delivers adrenaline during a severe allergic reaction.

clue.text: Underworld figure in Brussels flipped your chop

parts.note: Brussels is the seat of the European Union, EU

indicators.note: flipped turns the abbreviation over

parts.note: YR is the letter-writing abbreviation for your
to dice is to chop into cubes

explanation.surface: A gangland figure in Brussels makes a threat about a chop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld figure' suggests a gangster; here it is the Hades of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurydice, wife of Orpheus, died and was taken to Hades, from which he failed to rescue her.

clue.text: Spread fresh bun with pâté, say

indicators.note: fresh signals that bun and pâté are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, accents dropped
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: A fresh bread roll spread with pâté makes a snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanut butter is a paste spread on bread or toast.

clue.text: Turning grey immediately after turning yellow

indicators.note: the second turning flips the little word so it reads the other way

parts.note: on means immediately after, as in 'on arrival'
yellow and chicken both mean cowardly

explanation.surface: Someone's hair goes grey straight after a bout of jaundice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No chicken' is an idiom for someone no longer young; the first 'turning' belongs to the definition, the second is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a person is no chicken means they are past their youth, as someone going grey with age is.

clue.text: Group aboard Eurostar dines slowly, being delayed

indicators.note: the answer is a group of consecutive letters travelling aboard the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Eurostar, all of dines and the start of slowly

explanation.surface: A party on the cross-Channel Eurostar train takes its time over dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Tardiness is lateness, the state of running behind time.

clue.text: Loose nun cycles around Lot pregnant with son

indicators.note: around places the cycled letters either side of the rest
cycles moves the nun's first letter round to her end

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: pregnant with means carrying the son inside

parts.note: your lot in life is your fate

explanation.surface: A wayward nun on a bicycle circles Lot, who is expecting a son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' is a verb here, to set free, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose a knot or strap is to undo it, so the verb means release or untie.

clue.text: Official wheels daughter sobbing around abattoir on vacation

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car

indicators.note: around wraps the weeping word about the abattoir letters

parts.note: sobbing is crying

indicators.note: vacated, the abattoir is emptied of its middle, leaving its outer letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An official's car, carrying his crying daughter, swings round a deserted slaughterhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A card-carrying member is a registered, formally recognised one, so the word is an adjective meaning official.

clue.text: Charlie books ticket back to France, getting gite

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible
a tag is a label or ticket

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Charlie books a return ticket to France and takes a holiday let.
explanation.definitionFit: A gîte is a French holiday home, typically a rural house to rent, much like a country cottage.

clue.text: Train from Switzerland passing through bogs on the climb

indicators.note: the Swiss letters pass through the reversed toilets
in a down answer, climbing means reading upwards, so the word goes backwards

parts.note: bog and loo are British slang for a toilet
CH is Switzerland's international vehicle code

explanation.surface: A train from Switzerland climbs a mountain past marshland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a railway noun but is the verb, to teach.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to train or educate them.

clue.text: Nice to DC, relocating west

indicators.note: relocating moves the letters of the travel itinerary about

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone moves from Nice in France to Washington DC, heading west.
explanation.definitionFit: The Occident is the western world, as opposed to the Orient.

clue.text: A little fish learner always makes en croute?

indicators.note: en croute means in a pastry crust, so the always-word wraps the learner

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'

explanation.surface: A trainee chef is forever cooking fish in pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: An elver is a young eel, a small fish on its journey upriver.

clue.text: Estaminet I like that is west of the front line?

indicators.note: in an across answer, west means to the left, so these letters come first

parts.note: taken as written
so means in that way, like that
an estaminet is a small French cafe or bar

explanation.surface: A soldier in a First World War cafe near the front sighs that he likes it there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Estaminet' and 'front line' evoke the trenches; the line is really one on a weather chart, where fronts are drawn too.
explanation.definitionFit: An isobar is a line on a weather map joining points of equal pressure, drawn alongside the fronts.

clue.text: American opens ordinary wine, geared up for a row

indicators.note: the American letter opens up the wine, going inside it

parts.note: red is red wine

explanation.surface: An American uncorks plain wine, ready for an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with 'how' in the surface quarrel, but the answer means fitted with oars, the boating sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat that is oared is equipped with oars, ready to be propelled by rowing.

clue.text: Choice of route towards the centre of Dunkirk

parts.note: for can mean towards, as in heading for home

indicators.note: the centre of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A driver weighs routes on the way into Dunkirk town centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A fork in the road is where it splits, offering a choice of way.

clue.text: Six mistakes limiting a fellow's route in the Alps, say

indicators.note: the outer letters limit, or hem in, the article and the fellow

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
errata are listed mistakes in a printed book
taken as written
F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS; the 's links it to the route

explanation.surface: Six slips bound a man's climbing route in the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: A via ferrata is a protected mountain path with fixed cables and ladders, common in the Alps and Dolomites.

clue.text: Strolling aimlessly, finding patisserie by lake

indicators.note: by means beside, so the lake comes right next to the pastry

parts.note: a flan is a pastry tart, the kind of item a patisserie sells
Erie is one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A wanderer discovers a pastry shop beside a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Flânerie is the French idea of idle wandering about a city, the activity of the flâneur.

clue.text: These two gripping poles on chair lift

definitions.meaning: reads like two skiers holding their sticks, but describes the pair of porters holding the carrying poles
sounds like a ski-lift ride, but means the chair these people lift up

explanation.walkthrough: The skiing picture is a decoy: these are enclosed chairs carried on poles by two bearers, front and back.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedan chairs were enclosed seats carried by two porters holding poles, used for transport in the 1700s.
